routes.description: The pro route defends the Kalam by grounding the causal principle, arguing that a beginningless temporal series is metaphysically impossible, inferring that the universe began and therefore has a transcendent cause, and identifying personal agency as the best explanation of a timeless cause producing a temporal universe.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the expressed reasons support the causal principle and a finite past, thereby establishing a transcendent first cause, and if they exclude an eternal impersonal mechanism sufficiently to favor a personal creator.

bridges.description: The Kalam shows that the universe began to exist, has a transcendent cause, and points to a timeless, spaceless, immaterial, enormously powerful personal creator.
The past temporal series is finite and is not ontologically distinct from the universe, so the universe began to exist.
Whatever begins to exist has a cause because being cannot arise from non-being.
An actually infinite collection cannot exist concretely, so the series of past events cannot be actually infinite.
An eternal impersonal sufficient causal condition could not first produce a temporal universe finitely long ago, whereas a personal agent can freely initiate that effect.

routes.description: The con route argues that the Kalam's required inferences remain underdetermined: ordinary caused beginnings differ from an absolute material beginning, the peculiar behavior of infinite collections does not establish impossibility, a beginningless reality remains available, and impersonal or temporally structured alternatives weaken the inference to a personal creator.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if an indispensable causal, finite-past, or creator-identification inference remains unsupported or if a coherent beginningless or impersonal alternative prevents the Kalam from establishing its complete conclusion.

bridges.description: The Kalam does not establish its complete conclusion about a beginning, a cause, and a personal creator because at least one indispensable step remains open or false.
The philosophical objections to traversing or instantiating an infinite past do not establish that the past and universe are finite.
Caused beginnings observed in ordinary objects are rearrangements of existing material and therefore do not warrant a causal rule for an absolute beginning of material reality.
The strange behavior of infinite collections, including Hilbert's Hotel, does not by itself make their concrete existence metaphysically impossible.
Non-metric time, impersonal indeterministic causation, and difficulties with changeless consciousness prevent an inference from a first cause to a timeless personal creator.

moves.speaker: Alex Malpass
moves.proposition: Ordinary cups, tables, bicycles, and similar things have caused beginnings only as rearrangements of pre-existing material; because an absolute beginning of material reality would be different in kind and has never been observed, those ordinary examples do not justify extending the causal principle to the universe.
moves.attributionBasis: The span continues Malpass's Prior-based distinction after Craig's brief assent at event 241, and Craig begins his response at event 269.
moves.selectionRationale: This first-quartile span is a bounded argument against the pro route's causal-principle bridge and supplies enough contrast to identify one proposition without importing a separate argument.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: If there is not anything, then not anything can come into being; being comes only from being rather than from non-being, which grounds the requirement that something beginning to exist must have a cause.
moves.attributionBasis: The span is Craig's direct reply to Malpass's challenge at events 535-543 and uses Craig's stated Parmenidean rationale before the moderator intervenes.
moves.selectionRationale: This first-quartile passage compactly states the metaphysical inference behind the pro causal bridge as one recoverable proposition.

moves.speaker: Alex Malpass
moves.proposition: A Humean bundle account permits personal identity to be Pickwickish, while on Craig's substance-dualist account the soul portion of a person allegedly existed before the person's bodily beginning.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator's question at events 602-614 is answered continuously by Malpass, and Craig interrupts at event 637 to challenge Malpass's claim about the soul.
moves.selectionRationale: This second-quartile argumentative claim addresses Craig's example about composite substances but does not itself support or attack any stated bridge concerning the universe's cause, an infinite past, or creator properties.

moves.speaker: Alex Malpass
moves.proposition: If nothing can come from nothing and something exists now, then there could never have been nothing; Malpass therefore favors the conclusion that something, probably material reality, has always existed and that the universe has no beginning.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly addresses Alex at events 696-702, after which Malpass states his view continuously until Craig responds at event 739.
moves.selectionRationale: This second-quartile span gives a self-contained positive reason for rejecting an indispensable part of the complete Kalam conclusion without duplicating the con route's narrower infinity bridges.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: A beginningless temporal series would contain an actually infinite number of past events; because such a concrete actual infinite is impossible, the past series is finite and began, and because that series is not ontologically distinct from the universe, the universe began to exist.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator asks Bill to present his philosophical reasons at events 784-787, and this span is Craig's uninterrupted first argument.
moves.selectionRationale: This second-quartile passage states the full finite-past inference supporting the pro central bridge in a single bounded argument.

moves.speaker: Alex Malpass
moves.proposition: Hilbert's Hotel would behave strangely by accommodating new guests despite every room being occupied, but strangeness or absurdity is not equivalent to metaphysical impossibility, just as a platypus can be strange without being impossible.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly asks Alex about the scenarios at events 943-946, and Malpass answers continuously throughout the selected span.
moves.selectionRationale: This second-quartile span isolates Malpass's direct undercutting inference against the pro claim that Hilbert-style behavior establishes the impossibility of concrete actual infinities.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: Malpass himself relies on metaphysical intuitions in advancing a material-causation principle, an existence-exclusion principle, and a principle connecting countability of each event with countability of all events.
moves.attributionBasis: Craig begins his reply at event 1099, directly addresses Alex in this span, and cites positions he attributes to Malpass before Malpass resumes later.
moves.selectionRationale: This second-quartile dialectical criticism is important to their exchange but is compatible with every bridge being true or false, so it provides a deliberate no-contact candidate.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: No scientifically plausible impersonal indeterministic account explains a nonphysical state producing the universe only finitely long ago: a metastable impersonal condition with any eternal chance of producing it would do so from eternity or not at all, making personal explanation the appropriate category.
moves.attributionBasis: Malpass finishes presenting impersonal indeterministic causation at event 2351, and this span is Craig's direct continuous reply defending personal agency.
moves.selectionRationale: This fourth-quartile span supplies one explicit inference from the timing problem for an eternal impersonal cause to the pro route's personal-cause bridge.
